one_liner: Community Rust solution to the related-posts benchmark, about 1.28x faster than the suite's C++ solution on one core.
what_it_does: A roughly 100-line Rust program (rust/src/main.rs) that reads posts with tags, builds a tag-to-post-index map, counts shared tags for every other post, and keeps the top 5 related posts per post before writing JSON. It is a benchmark entry, not a library: there is no API, but the body of main between the two Instant::now() calls is a self-contained routine you could lift. JSON goes through serde_json with borrowed &str fields, outside the timed region.
how_it_is_fast: Same algorithm as cpp/main.cpp, which was ported from the Rust code in Sept 2024 ('copy rust algorithm, process every cacheline'): per-tag Vec<u32> of post indices, a u8 shared-tag counter per post, a scan in 64-byte chunks that skips a chunk unless some count exceeds the running 5th-best, and insert-and-bubble top-5. The counter buffer is a 64-byte-aligned AVec padded to a multiple of 64, the chunk scan uses slice iterators (no per-element bounds checks), and since Feb 2026 each chunk is zeroed right after it is scanned instead of a whole-array fill. The C++ entry runs the same steps with std::vector::at() on every counter access, a full memset per post and std::unordered_map; the suite publishes no profile, so which difference carries the gap is not documented.
when_to_use: As a reference pattern for sparse co-occurrence top-k (posts by tags, items by features) where one row of u8 counters fits in L1/L2: the measured sizes are 5k to 60k items
Single-core batch jobs with 4-5 tags per item from a small vocabulary (the generator draws from 28 tags), the measured shape
When end-to-end memory and JSON time matter too: the raw results show 29 MB peak RSS and 1.27-1.32 s whole-process at 60k posts versus 460 MB and 3.35-3.40 s for the C++ entry (nlohmann/json DOM)
Small inputs: at 5k posts it has the suite's best single-core time (9.84 ms versus D v2 12.06 ms and C++ 12.20 ms)
when_not_to_use: As evidence that Rust beats C++: the C++ entry is a port of this algorithm held to .at() everywhere and a separate memset, and nothing in the Rust code (u8 counters, chunk scan, fused zeroing) is beyond standard C++
Multicore runs: C++ Concurrent (402.33 ms total) beats Rust Concurrent (489.91 ms), and the separate Rust HO entry (51.55 ms) uses specialised data structures
Items that can share more than 255 tags: counters are u8 and would wrap (the suite caps tags at 100 per post)
Library integration: hard-coded ../posts.json and ../related_posts_rust.json paths, unwrap() on parse errors, and no API
Large vocabularies with long tag lists per item, where the per-post counter scan (O(n) per post, O(n^2) total) dominates; that shape was not measured

integration.dependencies: hashbrown 0.14.3 (ahash 0.8.7 default hasher), aligned-vec 0.5.0; serde 1 and serde_json 1.0.111 for JSON I/O only
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 2021 edition; usize::next_multiple_of needs Rust 1.73+ (inferred from the API used). The suite builds with rustup stable, version unstated
integration.platforms: any Rust target; measured on x86-64 (AWS c7a.xlarge) with no target-cpu flag
integration.thread_safety: single-threaded program; a separate rust_con (Rayon) variant exists for the multicore table

gotchas: The Rust and C++ rows come from separate container runs (Rust raw results committed 2026-02-11, C++ refreshed 2026-02-24), and docker_start.sh regenerates the 20k and 60k posts.json with gen_fake_posts.py, which calls random.sample without a seed, so the two rows were timed on different random datasets of the same distribution; verify.py checks output only on the 5k round (fixed posts.json).

The lead predates the fused chunk-zeroing commit (a9d2d27, Feb 2026): in the May 2025 run (Ubuntu 22.04 host), when Rust still zeroed the whole array after each scan like C++'s memset, Rust was 1.30 s versus C++ 1.72 s at 60k posts (about 1.32x, derived from page data). So the gap does not come from that trick, and the suite has not isolated what does (candidates are .at() in the C++ scan and insert loops, unordered_map, and the C++ build without LTO).

The C++ timer truncates to whole milliseconds (duration_cast<milliseconds>; raw values are 12 or 13 ms at 5k posts), which biases the C++ 5k figure low by up to 1 ms, so if anything Rust's 5k lead is understated. The Rust hot increment still uses bounds-checked indexing, as the suite's no-unchecked rule requires.
If fewer than 5 other posts share a tag, the unfilled top-5 slots stay (0, 0) and point at post 0, which can be the post itself; the C++ entry behaves the same and the suite's data never triggers it.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Among the same-suite siblings, pick it for the smallest inputs (fastest at 5k posts, 9.84 ms) or a Rust codebase; D (v2) is faster at 60k posts (961.08 ms versus 1.10 s) and on the total (1.10 s versus 1.23 s), and C3 trails at 1.28 s. Treat all three as implementation comparisons, not language results.
verified_claims_summary: On an AWS c7a.xlarge (CPU model not stated), mean processing time without JSON I/O was 9.84 / 124.59 / 1,100 ms for 5k / 20k / 60k posts (10, 3 and 3 runs) for Rust built by cargo --release with fat LTO, codegen-units 1 and panic=abort (stable toolchain, version unstated), versus 12.20 / 164.33 / 1,393 ms for the C++ entry built with Arch Linux clang++ -O3 -std=c++20 (no LTO, no -march, clang version unstated): about 1.28x on the totals (derived from page data). Whole-process times including JSON are 1.27-1.32 s versus 3.35-3.40 s at 60k posts.
status_note: The suite (served as zupat/related_post_gen after a transfer from jinyus, 500 stars, MIT) is maintained, with Rust results from 2026-02-11 after a Feb 2026 code change; it is a copyable reference pattern, not a maintained library.
